claims.text: Superconductivity emerges when local lattice ordering sufficiently reduces electron scattering caused by random chemical disorder.
Reduced disorder-driven electron scattering enhances the electron-phonon coupling needed for Cooper pairing.
The as-cast alloy has highly random atomic-site occupation.
Random atomic-site occupation in the as-cast alloy is associated with lattice distortions.
Annealing below the recrystallization threshold can promote local short-range chemical ordering without phase segregation.
The proposed annealing partially relaxes lattice distortions.
The proposed annealing develops short-range chemical ordering.
Relaxed lattice distortions and short-range ordering decrease electron-scattering centers.
Decreased impurity-like electron scattering improves electron-phonon interactions.
Improved electron-phonon interactions permit the formation and coherence of Cooper pairs.
Severe chemical randomness in the as-cast state suppresses superconductivity through pair-breaking scattering.
The untreated as-cast alloy has no superconducting transition and exhibits only normal metallic conduction at low temperature.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a superconducting transition in the 0–10 K test range.
The predicted superconducting transition will produce zero electrical resistance.
The predicted superconducting transition will produce an observable Meissner effect.
The mechanism applies only while the alloy remains chemically single-phase and annealing produces moderate local ordering.
Phase segregation caused by over-annealing, or insufficient ordering caused by under-annealing, can prevent the proposed effect.
Localized magnetic moments arising from particular elemental interactions could complicate the superconducting transition.
